opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's one of the questions at the heart of the Alberta Plan.

The short answer is that learning and acting shouldn't be separate phases at all. A lot of machine learning still works like this: you collect a big dataset, train a model offline, freeze it, and deploy it. In the Alberta Plan we take the opposite view. The agent is always learning, always acting, and always planning, all at the same time, for as long as it exists. There's no moment where someone says "training's over, now go perform."

We sometimes call this temporal uniformity. Every moment of the agent's life is treated the same way. Each time step, the agent takes in an observation, updates what it knows, makes predictions, maybe does a little planning, and chooses an action. Then it does it all again. Learning isn't something that happens to the agent before it meets the world. It's something the agent does because it's in the world.

That has real consequences for how you build things. If the agent is learning continually, its algorithms have to be incremental and computationally bounded. It can't stop and reprocess its entire history every time something new happens. It has to cope with a world that's much bigger and more complex than it is, which means its understanding will always be approximate. And because the world keeps changing, it needs to keep adapting rather than converge once and stop.

For me this isn't abstract. A lot of my work has been with prosthetic limbs and other assistive devices that people wear every day. Those devices really bring the point home. A person's body changes, their goals change, the sensors shift a bit on the skin. A device trained once in the lab and frozen just isn't going to keep up. What you want is a system that learns alongside the person, minute by minute and day by day. It builds predictions about what's going to happen next and uses them to act more helpfully, and its own actions keep shaping what it learns.

So in the Alberta Plan, acting is how the agent gathers the experience it learns from, and learning is how it gets better at acting. They're two sides of one ongoing loop that runs for the agent's whole lifetime. I think that loop is where real intelligence comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent updates what it knows at each time step and keeps learning from experience throughout its life; it also says learning must be incremental.

r002.rationale: It states that learning and acting are not separate phases, but happen together continuously for the agent’s whole lifetime.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. The short answer is that in the Alberta Plan, learning and acting aren't two separate phases. They're the same ongoing process, happening at every single time step, for the entire life of the agent.

A lot of the way we've traditionally built AI systems looks like this: you gather a big dataset, you train a model offline, you freeze it, and then you deploy it to act in the world. Learning happens first, acting happens second. The Alberta Plan deliberately rejects that separation. The agent we have in mind is a continual learner. It wakes up, it starts receiving a stream of observations and rewards, it takes actions, and it is updating itself from that experience moment to moment, for as long as it exists. There's no point where learning stops and "real" operation begins.

Part of why we care so much about this is that the world is non-stationary. If you're a robot, or a prosthetic limb, or any system embedded in a real environment with real people, things change. The user's body changes, the task changes, the sensors degrade. An agent that only learned once will slowly become mismatched to its circumstances. An agent that's always learning can keep pace with that drift.

The other piece is that acting is what generates the data you learn from. The experience stream is the ground truth. So the agent's actions shape what it gets to learn, and what it learns shapes how it acts. That loop is the whole point. In the plan we lay this out step by step: start with the basic agent that learns and acts online, build up predictive knowledge through things like general value functions, then add planning with a learned model, and eventually get to agents whose learning is itself driven by their own experience and their own choices about what to attend to.

One thing I'd stress, coming from my own work on prosthetics, is that this way of thinking matches how we actually want to live alongside these systems. A person with a limb difference doesn't want to retrain a device every time something shifts. They want something that adapts with them, continuously, over years. So the lifelong, always-learning, always-acting view isn't just an abstract design principle. It's about what makes an intelligent system a good long-term partner.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent continually updates itself from its ongoing stream of observations, rewards, and experience moment to moment, conveying incremental updates to its knowledge.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes learning and acting as the same ongoing process at every time step throughout the agent’s entire life.

astra-6.text:
I think learning and acting have to be intertwined throughout the agent’s lifetime. It’s not that you learn everything first and then go out into the world and act. You act with the knowledge you have, those actions produce new experience, and that experience changes what you know and how you act next.

In the Alberta Plan, that ongoing interaction is central. The agent is continually learning to predict what will happen, learning which actions are useful, and building representations that support both. And its behavior determines what it gets an opportunity to learn. So learning and acting aren’t separate stages; they’re parts of one continuing process that should make the agent more capable over its lifetime.

r001.rationale: The response says actions produce new experience and that this experience changes what the agent knows and how it acts next, describing ongoing updates to its knowledge.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says learning and acting are intertwined throughout the agent’s lifetime and parts of one continuing process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think learning and acting have to be interwoven throughout the agent’s lifetime. You don’t learn a model, freeze it, and then go off and act in the world. Acting generates the experience from which you learn, and what you learn changes how you act next. That loop continues for as long as the agent is operating.

In the Alberta Plan, that means taking continual learning seriously from the beginning. The agent has to build and update its understanding while it is pursuing goals, with limited computation and a stream of experience that it doesn’t get to choose independently of its actions. And its actions can serve both purposes: making progress on a task and gathering information that will make it more capable later.

So I’d see learning as part of the agent’s ongoing activity, rather than a separate preparation phase. The challenge is to make that relationship productive over a lifetime, so experience keeps improving the agent’s ability to predict, to make decisions, and to adapt.

r001.rationale: It says the agent builds and updates its understanding while pursuing goals from an ongoing stream of experience, communicating incremental updates to existing knowledge.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says learning and acting are interwoven throughout the agent’s lifetime and describes how each shapes the other.
